The course examines how the operation of different institutions and actors (public and private police, prosecution, courts, defendants, juries, corrections) shape the boundaries of the criminal law, focusing on the role of discretion and public interest/policy considerations.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe key principles underpinning the criminal law, particularly the concept of criminal responsibility.
Understand how the criminal law operates in relation to specific offences, defences, and contexts.
Analyse and critically evaluate the criminal law within specific situations, contexts, and crime types.
Apply effective legal research skills, such as analysis of case law, legislation, and secondary sources, to understand the application of the law and to support arguments re: law reform.
Demonstrate and apply skills required to communicate effectively within a legal and policy context.
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Criminal Law: Principles, Offences and Defences
syllabus_overview: This course involves the study of the general principles of criminal responsibility in the context of specific offences and defences under Queensland's criminal law. The course also introduces students to the criminal justice process and Australian criminal justice institutions.

title: Criminal Law and Procedure A
syllabus_overview: Criminal Law & Procedure A involves the study of the general principles of criminal responsibility & of specific offences & defences under Queensland's criminal law. The course draws comparisons - where relevant - to developments at common law. It also introduces the rapidly expanding area of federal criminal law.
workload_hours: Seminar 2 Hours/ Week Contact 1 Hour/ Week

title: Law of Torts I
syllabus_overview: This course considers the nature of the law of tort. It examines intentional torts against the person, and torts in relation to land and the enjoyment of land. The course also includes an introduction to the tort of negligence (including modification by the Civil Liability Act 2003 (Qld)).
learning_outcomes: Articulate the key concepts and principles in the law of torts.
Engage thoughtfully with case law and statutes.
Analyse facts and identify legal solutions to the problems raised by those facts.
Structure and communicate legal argument.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Trusts and Equity I
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to the nature and history of the equitable jurisdiction and to the law of trusts, focusing upon the creation of trusts, both testamentary and inter vivos. It also considers the classification of trusts, and commercial and other applications of trusts.

title: Trusts and Equity II
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the administration of trusts. Resulting and constructive trusts are also dealt with, but the main focus of the course is on the powers and duties of trustees and remedies in respect of breaches of trust. Related areas of law, in particular the law of fiduciary obligations and remedies in respect of breaches of such obligations are also considered in detail.
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Interests in Property
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon Foundations of Property Law but focuses exclusively on property rights and interests, both legal and equitable.
learning_outcomes: Identify and recall the principles and rules of property law.
Identify and apply property law principles in analysing particular factual situation.
Analyse and interpret relevant case law and statutes relating to property.
Demonstrate skills in written communication (including organising and structuring ideas) in the context of providing advice on legal issues related to property law.
Collaborate in a team to analyse property law issues, provide legal advice and reflect on professional practices.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Memorandum of Advice Team or group-based
Partner Briefing: Revised Legal Analysis and Advice Team or group-based

workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Foundations of Property Law
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the basic conceptual building blocks of the modern law of property in Australia (and, where necessary, in Queensland in particular). It explores the conceptual core of "property" in general, before systematically examining foundational concepts, rules, principles and operations (legal, equitable and statutory) relating to the two primary forms of property: personal property and real property.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge of, and an ability to identify and recall the fundamental principles and rules of, property law.
Identify and apply property-law principles in analysing particular factual situations.
Analyse and interpret relevant case law and statutes relating to property law.
Demonstrate skills in legal research (including an ability to identify and locate relevant literature) and demonstrate skills in written communication (including organising and structuring ideas).
Reflect upon the social implications of rules of property and critically evaluate common justifications for property rights.
workload_hours: Lecture 1 Hour/ Week Seminar 2 Hours/ Week

title: Criminal Law
syllabus_overview: This course critically explores the purpose and operation of criminal law in Australia, chiefly in Queensland. It covers the general principles of criminal liability, selected specific offences under Queensland's criminal law, and draws comparisons to developments at common law, federal criminal law, and other jurisdictions. The course also offers a brief introduction to criminal procedure.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sound understanding of the sources, principles, offences, and defences of criminal law in Australia, especially in Queensland.
Demonstrate a basic understanding of the sources, offences, and defences of criminal law in Australia, especially in Queensland.
Recognise the impact criminal law and criminal justice has on victims of crime, on Indigenous Australians, on society, on perpetrators, on human rights, and on criminal justice authorities.
Critically and independently analyse relevant laws, judicial decisions, policy documents, and academic writing in this field of study.
Independently create solutions and develop recommendations for policy change and law reform.
workload_hours: Lecture 1 Hour/ Week Seminar 2 Hours/ Week

title: Occupational Health & Safety Law
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to the central legal concepts and principles in occupational health and safety, including the history and development of OH&S legislation, the relationship between OH&S law and industrial law, and the relationship between OH&S legislation and common law.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Assignment, Plan, Role Play, Case Review

workload_hours: Contact 24 Hours/ One Off 4 Day Intensive over two weekends.

title: Law of Property A
syllabus_overview: This course is an intermediate level analysis of the law and policy of Australian property law which introduces students to fundamental principles and concepts. The course comprises a study of possession and title to land, the doctrines of tenure and estates, concurrent ownership, leasehold interests, strata title and additionally introduces students to native title. The course seeks to develop students' knowledge and understanding in these areas, and their ability to solve complex legal problems.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Trusts and Equity
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the concept of 'equity' as a distinct body of law and discusses the historical reasons for its development. It considers the equitable rules relating to the creation and classification of trusts, the duties and powers of trustees, and the remedies available to enforce them. It also considers the equitable rules relating to fiduciary duties.
learning_outcomes: Explain the rules and principles of law relating to the creation of trusts, and the duties, powers, rights and liabilities of trustees and persons in fiduciary positions.
Apply those rules and principles to concrete fact situations.
Read and analyse case and statute law in these areas of law.
Undertake research in these areas of law with a view to resolving more complex problems or critically evaluating the law.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Corporations Law
syllabus_overview: A practice-oriented introduction to Australian corporate and business associations law for commerce students. The course focuses on how business structures allocate rights, duties and risk, with particular emphasis on companies: incorporation and corporate personality; corporate finance fundamentals; governance and decision-making; directors¿ duties; shareholder rights and remedies; and corporate distress/external administration. Students learn to work with primary sources (Corporations Act, cases, regulator guidance) and to communicate structured solutions to commercially realistic problems.
learning_outcomes: Explain the key features and consequences of common business structures, particularly the company form.
Apply company law principles (governance, finance, duties, remedies, insolvency triggers) to solve structured problems.
Evaluate legal risk and compliance options for typical corporate decisions (board, management, shareholders).
Communicate well-structured legal advice/analysis for business audiences using appropriate authorities and conventions.
Use legal information environments independently to locate current law and recognise ethical dimensions (e.g. governance failures, conflicts, disclosure) in corporate problem-solving.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Income Tax Law
syllabus_overview: A skills-based introduction to Australian income tax, Goods and Services Tax (GST) and Fringe Benefits Tax (FBT) for future accounting and tax professionals, focusing on the application of legislation, case law and Australian Taxation Office (ATO) rulings in that context. The course explicitly develops workplace capabilities: structured legal reasoning, accuracy, business-focused and financial decision-making, and effective communication in a rapidly changing regulatory field.
learning_outcomes: Identify and apply sources of taxation law and administration (legislation, cases, ATO guidance) to practical problems.
Communicate reasoned tax positions (including uncertainty/risk) to non-legal audiences in professional form.
Construct annotated calculations of the taxable income and taxes payable of a range of taxpayers.
Evaluate and explain the income tax implications of non-complex international transactions.
Evaluate and explain the GST implications of business transactions and the FBT implications of employment entitlements.
Demonstrate professional responsibility, including ethical decision-making and compliance awareness.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Law of Property B
syllabus_overview: This course is an intermediate level analysis of the law of real and personal property interests in Australia. The course builds on the fundamental principles and concepts related to property that are considered in Property Law A. The course comprises a study of statutory schemes relating to property: the Torrens Title system to land and the Personal Property Securities Act in relation to personal property. It also examines equitable interests in property and proprietary interests in real and personal property. The course seeks to deepen students' knowledge in these areas and their ability to solve complex legal problems related to interests in property.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Law of Trusts B
syllabus_overview: Administration of trusts and deceased estates, including consideration of duties and powers of trustees and executors, variation of trusts, trustees' right to indemnity, remedies for breach of trust. Consideration of situations in which resulting trusts arise.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Transnational Crime and International Criminal Justice
syllabus_overview: Transnational Crime and International Criminal Justice explores the levels and patterns of organised crime and associated crime types and critically examines the international law and national policies to prevent and suppress these phenomena. The course is interactive and allows students to independently research specific crime types, engage in discussion, and present their findings and opinions.
learning_outcomes: Have a general understanding of the patterns and levels of transnational organised crime and terrorism.
Describe and critique the nature and problems of transnational organised crime and terrorism.

Identify key instruments and the strengths and weaknesses of the current system of international criminal justice, especially as it relates to the criminalisation of transnational crime and terrorism and enforcement.
Navigate the complexity of international and transnational legal, policy, and institutional contexts in order to be able to effectively engage with key debates emerging in this area.

Work together with others to identify the dimensions of a problem arising from a case study of global or transnational crime, to generate solutions to the problem, and to communicate this to an informed audience.
Apply skills required to engage in effective legal and academic research, and to communicate effectively within a legal and policy context.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Online test 1 Identity Verified In-person Online
Group research project Team or group-based Online
Online test 2 Identity Verified In-person Online

workload_hours: Seminar 6 Hours/ Week Seminar 5 Hours/ Fortnight

title: Ethics and the Legal Profession
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with information about the history and development of the legal profession, and current structures and bodies that regulate lawyers today. The course examines in detail the law, professional rules and values applying to lawyers, and explores ethical issues that arise in professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain the law and rules of conduct and regulatory processes applicable to the legal profession (with particular reference to Queensland) and its rules of conduct.
Explain the legal requirements applicable to lawyers for dealing with trust money.
Apply knowledge of legal ethics to the practise of law, drawing on prominent philosophies and the moral and societal importance for ethical conduct by lawyers.
Reflect on your personal ethical framework, how it relates to and impacts on important aspects of legal practice.
Apply advanced decision-making skills to ethical issues arising in legal practice.
workload_hours: Lecture 1 Hour/ Week Workshop 2 Hours/ Week

title: Law of Torts II
syllabus_overview: This course builds on the basic knowledge of the law of torts developed in Torts I, focusing in greater depth on particular problem areas within the law of negligence. It also introduces students to a further range of torts protecting personal interests and places the law of torts in context by examining principles of vicarious liability and alternative compensation schemes that exist for personal injury and death.
learning_outcomes: Identify key tort liability issues.
Identify the rules and principles of tort law, including the primary sources of law (case authorities and statutory provisions).
Identify and critique the moral and policy values underpinning tort law.
Engage in the evaluation and creative criticism of tort law and legalpolicy.
Apply tort law effectively to solve unfamiliar problems and produce well-reasoned legal advice in areas of legal uncertainty.
Communicate legal advice effectively in written English, observing appropriate professional conventions and legal citation practices.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Administrative Law
syllabus_overview: This course is concerned with the legal accountability of bodies wielding public power or discharging public functions to ensure that people's rights and interests are respected in their dealings with governments and their delegates or agents. Public power encompasses administrative, judicial and legislative power, and this course is primarily concerned with accountability for the exercise of administrative (executive) power in a range of settings.
learning_outcomes: Identify, explain and evaluate the different ways in which bodies exercising public power are held legally accountable.
Understand and critically explain how Administrative Law relates to Constitutional Law and Human Rights Law.
Appreciate the differences between 'merits review' (often exercised by administrative tribunals) and judicial review (via the courts) where the 'legality' of decision-making is examined.
Identify, explain and apply relevant legal rules and principles of judicial review - in particular, the grounds for judicial review, jurisdiction to review and remedies.
Be critically aware of historical and contemporary problems/controversies within the discipline (including automated decision-making).
Undertake independent legal research relevant to the discipline.
workload_hours: Lecture 1 Hour/ Week Seminar 2 Hours/ Week

title: Constitutional Law
syllabus_overview: This course continues the study of state and federal constitutional law introduced in Principles of Public Law. The course examines the constitutional relationship between the states and the Commonwealth, the subjects of Commonwealth legislative and executive power, constitutional principles concerning the separation of powers and judicial independence, constitutional rights and freedoms, and the amendment of the state and Commonwealth Constitutions.
learning_outcomes: Explain and evaluate the ways in which federalism is embodied in the Australian federal Constitution.
Explain and apply the basic principles of constitutional interpretation including the legislative, executive and judicial powers of the Commonwealth.
Explain and apply the law in relation to Commonwealth-state relations.
Explain and apply the rights and liberties expressly or impliedly secured by the Constitution.
Explain and evaluate the ways in which constitutional change is effected under the federal and state constitutions.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Jurisprudence
syllabus_overview: This course offers an overview of some of the main historical, doctrinal and philosophical perspectives that have influenced the understanding of law as an institution, together with an introduction to key theoretical positions and interdisciplinary movements that provide critique and commentary on the role of law.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the central ideas and assumptions underlying major jurisprudential traditions, including their historical development and contemporary relevance.
Critically evaluate and compare competing theoretical perspectives on law, justice, morality, and authority, using advanced critical reasoning and intellectual independence.
Communicate jurisprudential arguments clearly, coherently, and persuasively in formats appropriate for academic or professional contexts, demonstrating ethical engagement with diverse perspectives.
Reflect on the normative, ethical, and socio-cultural implications of different theories of law, including their significance for legal practice, justice, and Australian law.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Law of Trusts A
syllabus_overview: Introduction to the nature & history of the equitable jurisdiction & to the law of trusts, focusing upon the creation of trusts, both testamentary & inter vivos. Classification of trusts & consideration of commercial & other applications of trusts.
prerequisites: All level 1 LAWS courses (LLB(Grad Entry) & LLB(Hons)(#48) students excepted) + LAWS2111 + LAWS2112
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Jurisprudence
syllabus_overview: Jurisprudence offers an overview of the historical, doctrinal & philosophical perspectives that have influenced the development of law, together with an introduction to key theoretical positions & interdisciplinary movements that provide critique and commentary on the role of law. Topics include theoretical accounts of the nature of law (including the theories of Hart, Dworkin, Austin, and Kelsen); the central ideas of the natural law tradition, the nature of legal reasoning & the role of the judge; the analytical nature of legal rights & duties; conceptions of justice; the internal organisation of the law; & an introduction to a range of theoretical perspectives of the law, both internal & external.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Corporate Law
syllabus_overview: A study of aspects of the law concerning companies, including the nature of corporate bodies, corporate personality & limited liability, formation, management & governance, finance, & liquidation.
workload_hours: Seminar 2 Hours/ Week Contact 2 Hours/

title: Law of Evidence
syllabus_overview: This course is a critical examination of the law and practice relating to evidence in civil and criminal proceedings in Queensland and under the uniform legislation operating in some other parts of Australia. The course involves an analysis of the underlying principles of the law of evidence, and involves an examination of contentious evidentiary issues through a comparative and international perspective.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the law of evidence in Queensland, including relevant case law and statutory provisions, and relevant comparative aspects of the law of evidence in other Australian jurisdictions.
Explain the underlying rationale for the main rules and principles of the law of evidence.
Apply the relevant rules, principles and strategies of the law of evidence to hypothetical situations.
Examine the effect of relevant procedural rules and strategic and practical considerations when applying the law of evidence in Queensland.
Critically evaluate the law of evidence in Queensland, its policy dimensions and operation in practice, including some comparison with the rules of evidence in other jurisdictions.
prerequisites: Pre-2026 commencing students: 24 units LAWS courses 2026 onwards: All level 1, 2 and 3 LAWS courses

assessment_tasks.task_name: Court Report (Video Presentation with Notes) Online

workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Civil Dispute Resolution
syllabus_overview: Please note this is a 2 unit course. Students who commenced in 2017 or 2018 may need to complete an additional level 5 LAWS elective to meet the requirements of their program (contact bel@uq.edu.au for advice). This course explores the processes of commencing, conducting and concluding civil disputes including State and Federal civil procedure, alternative dispute resolution, private international law and remedies. Issues of jurisdiction, costs of resolving disputes, the role of lawyers and the courts in managing civil disputes, defining the issues in dispute, obtaining evidence, disclosure, judgment and enforcement are all examined.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the key rules and principles relevant to each stage of a civil proceeding in Queensland.
Apply rules and principles of civil procedure law effectively to solve unfamiliar problems.

Evaluate a range of options available to a party in a civil matter and justify the most appropriate course in the circumstances with reference to relevant rules, principles and ethical considerations.
Critically analyse and evaluate civil procedure law, practice and policy.
Draw selected court documents and communicate legal advice effectively in written English, observing appropriate professional conventions and, where appropriate, citation practices.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Pleading - Settle a Statement of Claim Online

workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Comparative Constitutional Law
syllabus_overview: The course offers insights into worldwide constitutional systems, providing theoretical and practical bases for understanding, evaluating, and comparing different constitutions. It focuses on constitutional theory and practices, examining how principles manifest in supranational, federal, and devolutionary systems.
learning_outcomes: Identify an appropriate methodology of comparative law.
Understand the fundamental principles underlying constitutional and federal theories.
Distinguish constitutions according to the appropriate typologies.
Compare and evaluate different constitutions worldwide.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: The Law of Estate Planning and Wealth Management
syllabus_overview: The course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the legal principles and regulations governing estate planning and wealth management in Australia. It develops students¿ ability to apply legal knowledge to practical estate planning scenarios, ensuring the effective protection and allocation of assets. It enhances students¿ skills in identifying, analysing, and resolving ethical and practical issues related to estate planning. It fosters critical thinking and innovative problem-solving skills in relation to the law of estate planning and wealth management.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: International Human Rights Law
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the fundamental principles and institutional framework of international human rights law. It examines the origins and development of human rights in international law, jurisdiction and the nature of States' obligations, limitations to human rights, and mechanisms for enforcement, as well as key critiques and emerging challenges in this area of international law.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: AI and the Law
syllabus_overview: This course provides a comprehensive overview of the legal implications of AI, including its potential to automate legal processes, introduce new forms of liability, and raise ethical dilemmas. Students will critically examine the challenges and opportunities presented by AI in various legal contexts and develop strategies for addressing these issues.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: Law, Justice, and the State
syllabus_overview: This course considers leading conceptions of justice advanced by political and legal theorists, and critiques thereof. It examines various moral values in terms of which legal and political institutions might be assessed. The moral values that it considers include liberty, community, utility, fairness, and equality. Among the themes that it explores are the limits of and connections between these ideals, the prospects for their realisation in contemporary societies, and the politics with which each is associated.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: Corporate Law
syllabus_overview: This course considers the law concerning companies, including the nature of corporate bodies, corporate personality and limited liability, formation, management and governance, finance, and liquidation.
learning_outcomes: Apply the rules governing the formation, operation, and dissolution of companies to hypothetical legal problems.
Explain to an intelligent layperson how those rules reflect ideas about society and the economy, as well as theories of regulation and corporate governance.
Undertake research to resolve more complex problems or analyse the impacts of actual or potential changes to the rules on company law.
Where relevant, incorporate normative and theoretical reflections into legal analysis in the area of company law.
prerequisites: LAWS1700, LAWS1701, LAWS1702, LAWS2706, LAWS2707, LAWS2709

assessment_tasks.task_name: 'Be my Clerk!' - Interactive Oral Assessment In-person

workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Climate Change Law in Australia
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the key legal issues involved with addressing climate change in Australia. This includes an introduction to the scientific and international legal contexts, as well as an analysis of legal regimes in Australia to regulate greenhouse gas emissions, corporate climate disclosures, and climate change adaptation and litigation.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: Intellectual Property Law
syllabus_overview: This course is an introduction and overview of intellectual property law. The course will cover philosophical, doctrinal, and critical approaches to understanding this domain, as well as introduce students to different forms of intellectual property including copyright, trademarks, designs, patents, cultural property, and more.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: Corporate Governance and Regulation
syllabus_overview: Corporate governance is a distinct field involving the mechanisms by which companies are controlled and directed, including legal, regulatory, administrative, and market-based practices. This course covers the allocation of rights and responsibilities among business participants and ensures accountability of those managing companies. It provides a focused, principled overview of governance arrangements in Australia, situated within broader policy and theoretical contexts shaping modern corporate governance law and practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain to an intelligent layperson the principles underlying the governance of corporations in Australia and internationally.
Understand and explain the theoretical bases of corporate governance and how the mechanisms of governance currently employed reflect theoretical conceptions of the corporation.
Analyse real or hypothetical situations and identify the doctrinal and normative governance issues arising from these situations.
Demonstrate an awareness of the different policy perspectives that bear upon the conceptualisation of corporate governance issues and their solutions.
Undertake research in the field of corporate governance with a view to resolving more complex problems or advising on the effect of further developing or reforming current principles and rules.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Elder Law
syllabus_overview: This course examines legal and ethical issues pertinent to Australia¿s older population; an increasingly important topic given Australia's ageing population and the growing prevalence of dementia. In particular, it explores the law and ethics relating to legal capacity, advance care planning, end-of-life decision-making, elder abuse, and aged care.
learning_outcomes: Apply legal and ethical concepts to issues facing older Australians, including in relation to capacity, advance care planning, end-of-life decision-making, elder abuse, and aged care.
Critically analyse the broader societal implications of legal and ethical issues facing older Australians, and the contrasting societal perspectives on these issues.
Communicate clearly and cogently in written and oral formats.
Work effectively in a team to apply knowledge of legal and ethical issues facing older Australians in a practical context.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written application Team or group-based Online
Oral presentation Team or group-based In-person

workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: Law and Society
syllabus_overview: The course explores the intricate relationship between law and society by examining the origins of legal and social norms, their various forms, and their impact on behaviour, social order, and change. This course draws on socio-legal scholarship and empirical studies to provide a comprehensive understanding of law in context, from foundational theories to diverse legal systems and contemporary legal practices.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: International Law-making in a Global World
syllabus_overview: This course examines various forms and instances of international law-making. It provides students with the tools to identify, describe and assess legal change within the global legal order. Students will be prepared to participate in international law-making processes as well as to deploy an array of legal norms as users of international law.
learning_outcomes: Analyse current issues and trends in international law-making.
Analyse and research key concepts and issues in international law.
Negotiate and draft international legal instruments.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Mock treaty negotiation Team or group-based In-person

workload_hours: Seminar 30 Hours/ Semester

title: Legal Design and Innovation
syllabus_overview: This course will give students experience in applying human-focused design thinking as a means of improving the legal system, legal services, and legal information. The course will examine some of the major trends shaping the design and delivery of legal services and will consider the role of lawyering and innovation in responding to these trends. It will provide an opportunity for students to engage in projects that explore change and disruption in the legal profession or legal system, and to consider how people with legal expertise can make justice more accessible for end-users. The course will equip students with knowledge and skills about the methods used to generate creative and useful changes to the justice system.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705 + permission from Head of School
workload_hours: Case Based Learning 30 Hours/ Semester

title: Legal Internships
syllabus_overview: The course provides students with the opportunity to gain practical legal skills and undertake a legal workplace experience that complements and deepens their coursework learning in the LLB(Hons) program.
learning_outcomes: Understand professional legal practice through engaging directly in legally-oriented work.
Understand and critically appreciate the role and value of lawyering in the context of the organisation where the internship is completed.
Understand the practice dimensions of the particular legal area relevant to the internship.
Have greater insight into their own learning and professional identity.
Bring critical insight into some of the challenges and opportunities facing lawyers and/or organisations and the social, financial, and legal frameworks within which they operate.
A deeper understanding of, and increased capacity to engage with, law, policy and reform in the area of the internship.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705 + permission from Head of School

assessment_tasks.task_name: Attendance at Placement (120 hours) AND Attendance at Teaching Workshops and Check-in Sessions In-person
Reflective Journal and Presentation In-person Online

workload_hours: Case Based Learning 30 Hours/ Semester

title: Family Law
syllabus_overview: This course is an intermediate level consideration and examination of, and reflection upon, the legal issues, legislation, case law, theory, practice, social context and key features of what is commonly known as "family law" in Australia. The course seeks to develop students' knowledge of the law relating to the breakdown of interpersonal relationships; awareness of the application of the relevant principles set out in the Family Law Act (and other related legislation including the Domestic and Family Violence Act) in both a legal and wider social context; and ability to identify and critically consider legal issues in the midst of complex inter-personal issues.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sound knowledge of both the law relating to the breakdown of marriages and de facto relationships and of the means for resolving disputes in relation to children, property division and maintenance.
Demonstrate knowledge of the legal institutions relevant to the practise of family law in Australia.
Demonstrate advanced written skills in the resolution of problems that arise in the context of family law.
Recognise the relationship between family law matters and those of other jurisdictions and areas of legal practice.
Critically analyse facts and provide solutions to theoretical and practical questions arising from the study of family law.

Situate family law within a broader social science context, recognising the influence of other disciplines (including psychology, gender and race studies and economics) on the theory and practice of family law.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fact sheet and legal advice Online
Making a parliamentary inquiry submission as a legal organisation Online

workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Semester Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Labour Law
syllabus_overview: This course is focused on the federal law regulating employment. The course seeks to develop student awareness of this practical and important area, covering both individual and collective aspects, and common law, constitutional and statutory issues. It also places the black-letter law in its political context, including the balance between employee protection and economic efficiency.
learning_outcomes: Sketch the evolution of the Australian labour law system, and the constitutional, workplace relations and industrial political factors underlying it.
Understand the national statutory regime (The Fair Work Act) and its key obligations and freedoms, in the context of the common law contractual framework.
Describe the mechanisms and parameters for fixing employment conditions and obligations under the national system.
Appreciate the role of key regulatory institutions, such as the Fair Work Commission and trade unions.
Apply specific knowledge acquired in the course to answer both hypothetical questions (particularly on dismissal law) and engage in longer, more critical debates about labour law.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written assignment - hypothetical advice on a contract of employment Online
Oral presentation - opening statements and discussion in a mock conciliation format (group work) Team or group-based In-person

workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Medical Law
syllabus_overview: The law as it relates to selected aspects of medicine and medical practice including medical negligence, medical battery, abortion, euthanasia, property rights in human body parts, competency determinations and product liability.
learning_outcomes: Describe some of the current controversies in medicine and the law; and
Analyse the legal consequences arising out of a doctor-patient interaction.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Human Rights Law
syllabus_overview: This course is a critical examination of the legal and social issues that arise in the practice of human rights law. The course seeks to develop students' skills in critical analysis by encouraging them to reflect on the role of human rights law in protecting vulnerable people, shaping legislation and influencing public policy, and whether human rights law has the capability to solve complex social problems.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of human rights laws (including anti-discrimination laws) and be able to apply them in domestic legal situations.
Determine the kinds of remedies that are available to defend human rights in a variety of domestic legal situations.
Appreciate the manner in which the law impacts upon vulnerable groups in Australia.
Work in a team to develop skills in human rights lawyering.
Apply a 'rights-based' approach to legal practice.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Phone a friend Team or group-based Online

workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Media Law
syllabus_overview: This course is an intermediate level examination of the legal and regulatory issues pertaining to Media Law in Australia and internationally. The course seeks to develop students' awareness of the complex issues inherent in the regulation of the Media and newsgathering and reportage practices and new media regulation.
learning_outcomes: Understand the concept of freedom of communication and its significance in determining the rights of the media to access and publish information.

Understand laws that restrict the medias access to and publication of information including defamation, injurious falsehood, misleading and deceptive conduct, passing off, the law of contempt, common law protection for privacy, and the law relating to confidential information, and laws that apply to offensive publications.
Analyse issues in media law in their historical and social context.
Be aware of the different approaches in a number of legal jurisdictions to the protection of rights and interests affecting the media.
Critically analyse claims by the media and others to legal protection.
Acquire the knowledge and analytical skills to advise media and other clients.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Planning and Development Law
syllabus_overview: The course is about planning and development law in Queensland, with a focus on the Planning Act 2016, the Planning Regulation 2017 and the Planning and Environment Court Act 2016 and related subordinate legislation and statutory instruments. The course seeks to provide students with an understanding of the statutory framework of planning and development law, and planning principles and practice.
learning_outcomes: An appreciation of the key planning instruments under the Planning Act 2016 (Qld), their role in planning and development assessment and their construction.
An ability to successfully navigate the development assessment system under the Planning Act 2016 (Qld).
A broad understanding of development assessment under the Planning Act 2016 (Qld) and the jurisprudence that underpins development assessment.
An understanding of the importance of infrastructure planning and charging under the Planning Act 2016 (Qld).
A familiarity with the practices, procedures and philosophy of the Queensland Planning and Environment Court.
A broad knowledge of the development enforcement regime.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Law and Indigenous Peoples
syllabus_overview: This course involves a study of the relevant laws and policies governing the rights of and the issues faced by the Indigenous peoples of Australia, both nationally and under international law. Additionally, this course affords the opportunity for a comparative study of the laws and policies governing Indigenous peoples in other parts of the world.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a strong general understanding of the historical and contemporary significance of law (Australian, Indigenous, international and comparative) for Indigenous peoples in Australia.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of some legal issues concerning Indigenous peoples.
Reflect critically on laws role in producing Indigenous peoples experiences of domination and injustice, and on laws potential role in overcoming such domination and injustice.
Undertake effective research into legal issues concerning Indigenous peoples.
Demonstrate skills in effective communication across a range of formats and audiences.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Environmental Law
syllabus_overview: This course is a critical examination and analysis of the legal, social and political contexts of environmental law in Australia. The course seeks to develop students' knowledge of environmental laws, and ability to solve complex legal problems and critically evaluate the effectiveness of environmental laws.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a broad knowledge of the principles that underpin environmental law in Australia.
Reflect on and engage in critical analysis of environmental law issues from a multi-disciplinary perspective.
Communicate to suit different contexts/audiences and in different forms.
Identify issues and explore solutions to theoretical and practical questions arising from the study of environmental laws at the Commonwealth and Queensland levels.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Presentation and Individual Reflection In-person

workload_hours: Lecture 1 Hour/ Week Seminar 2 Hours/ Week

title: Commercial Law
syllabus_overview: Commercial law addresses some of the issues which arise in commercial law practice such as agency, sale of goods, insurance, and business to business conduct.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the basic principles that inform commercial law.
Analyse and interpret case law and statute law relevant to commercial law.
Bring to bear, where appropriate, a critical appraisal of modern commercial law.
Identify and apply relevant legal principles in the analysis of a given factual situation, and present an appreciation of the legal position.
Take instructions and commence the drafting of a commercial agreement.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Competition Law
syllabus_overview: This course is a critical investigation into Australian competition law. The course seeks to develop students' knowledge of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) and ability to solve complex legal problems.
learning_outcomes: Understanding the principles underlying the provisions of Part IV of the CCA.
Interpret and explain relevant sections of Part IV of the CCA in the resolution of real or hypothetical situations.
Understand the development of the principles underlying Part IV of the CCA through the cases and the nature of proposals for their reform.
Explain, analyse and critically evaluate the principles of major cases in the resolution of real or hypothetical situations.
Undertake research in these areas of law with a view to resolving more complex problems or advising on the effect of further developing or reforming current laws and principles.
Demonstrate an ability to apply critical reasoning and independent judgement in an area of Australian competition law.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS course + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Lecture 1 Hour/ Week Seminar 2 Hours/ Week

title: Insurance Law
syllabus_overview: The course focuses on the statutes and common law principles regulating insurance law. The aim of the course is to familiarise students with legislation such as the Insurance Contracts Act 1984 (Cth) and compulsory third party motor vehicle workers compensation legislation as well as the common law principles applicable to insurance contracts.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

title: Consumer Law
syllabus_overview: This course is an advanced level examination of consumer law as an element of the Australian legal system generally, and consumer protection legislation and regulation in particular. Students will have their knowledge of consumer law enhanced and will be expected to apply and improve their analytical and communication skills in practical, social and theoretical contexts.
learning_outcomes: Understand the social, commercial and regulatory context that gave rise to a national consumer protection regime embodied in the Australian Consumer Law (“the ACL”).
Be able to describe and explain how and why the ACL is an important component of Australia’s overarching National Competition Policy.
Gain proficiency in identifying and navigating the different Chapters, Parts, Divisions, Subdivisions and Sections of the ACL.
In navigating the ACL, be able to accurately identify the relevant provisions and sequences of provisions within the ACL as they relate to specific consumer issues.

Be able to locate and understand relevant case law in interpreting provisions of the ACL and the application of that case law in formulating solutions to consumer protection issues, including relevant consumer remedies.
As part of that, understanding how the provisions of the ACL modify or abrogate traditional commercial / consumer relationships and associated remedies in contract, tort and equity.

Be aware of current and emerging consumer issues and how the ACL seeks to address those issues including an understanding of the role of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (“the ACCC”) in enforcing the ACL.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Lecture 1 Hour/ Week Workshop 2 Hours/ Week

title: Introduction to Taxation Law
syllabus_overview: Introduction to basic concepts of income tax legislation such as income, residence & source; timing of recognition of receipt of income; capital gains; allowable deductions & treatment of trading stock.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the regulatory framework of the income tax system in Australia.
Demonstrate an understanding of the components of the income tax equation which form the basis for determining an individual taxpayer's liability to pay income tax.
Interpret provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Acts to prepare a written argument that forms the basis of sound advice on a taxation matter.
Critically evaluate taxation judgements, Taxation Rulings and Taxation Determinations.
Discuss legal issues relating to taxation law in a confident and informed manner.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Succession Law
syllabus_overview: This course is an introductory level examination of law, legal issues, regulation, legislation, case law, and practice of succession in Australia, and in some overseas jurisdictions. The course seeks to develop students' knowledge of succession law and the ability to solve complex legal problems whilst examining proposals for reform.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an acceptable level of knowledge and understanding of the elements of Queensland succession law.
Communicate your knowledge of succession law effectively and appropriately, in writing and verbally.
Navigate independently through legal information environments, including online legal resources.
Use your knowledge of succession law to identify, analyse and solve complex legal problems.
Critically evaluate the role of succession law in contemporary society.
Appreciate your legal, social and professional responsibilities to your peers, your profession and your community.
prerequisites: All level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Conflict of Laws
syllabus_overview: The legal system of a State reflects its society's values. As a result, national laws and the structure of domestic judicial systems vary considerably. In an increasingly global and interconnected world legal situations or events arise that bring these different national systems into contact and conflict. This could be commercial transactions between entities in different States, marriage and other family law issues between nationals of different States, or torts in one State affecting nationals in other States. When such conflicts, or differences, arise in an Australian context, national laws and procedures need to be in place to resolve them. This course addresses such a conflict of laws in Australia in three parts: first, which State ought to have jurisdiction to adjudicate the dispute; second, which State's laws ought to apply to the dispute; and third, how a judgement from a court in one State might be recognised and enforced in another State.
learning_outcomes: Identify, restate and accurately explain in writing the general principles and rules of private international law, and the choice of law principles and rules relevant to the law of obligations.

Resolve or provide legitimate solutions to problems that give rise to issues that attract the operation of the general principles and rules of private international law, and the choice of law principles and rules relevant to the law of obligations.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Reflections on conflict of laws Online

workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Law and Technology
syllabus_overview: Legal and commercial rules and issues underpinning electronic commerce, including electronic banking, transnational electronic business transactions, electronic sale of goods and verification, cybercrime, jurisdictional issues and privacy.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the important principles, case law and legislation in the field of technology and the law.
Demonstrate both knowledge and legal reasoning of technology and the law through written and verbal processes.
Identify legal problems, demonstrate the ability to independently access legal resources, and think innovatively when faced with solving problems.
Evaluate the law of electronic commerce generally, as well as specific legal rules locally and nationally; demonstrate the ability to recognise areas for improvement in technology and the law.
Understand and appreciate the professional responsibilities to peers and the community.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Public International Law
syllabus_overview: Introduction to international law (including institutional structures, pacific settlement of disputes, history and theoretical assessments); sources of international law (with particular attention to treaties); international and municipal law; international personality (including States and international organisations); State jurisdiction and responsibility; international human rights law; international criminal law; international economic law; international environmental law; law of the sea; use of force and the law of armed conflict.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Maritime Law
syllabus_overview: Aspects of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction, including liens and arrest of ships, bills of lading, charter parties, marine insurance, securities, collisions and groundings, salvage, pilotage, towage, wreck, bounty and ransom.
learning_outcomes: identify, restate, explain and evaluate the fundamental principles of maritime law and their place in the Australian legal system;
understand and critically evaluate the operation of maritime law within the wider context of public international law and commercial law;

demonstrate a sound knowledge and understanding of the principles of maritime law, the legislation and conventions giving effect to those principles, and the body of case law which has developed and interpreted the principles; and
apply the principles and legal rules to practical legal issues.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: European Union Law
syllabus_overview: Introduction to constitutional, administrative & economic law of the European Union. Topics include Union Treaty, political & judicial institutions & protection of social rights by European Court of Justice.
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: International Trade Law
syllabus_overview: This course is an intermediate level elective which examines and seeks to develop students' knowledge and awareness of the law, practice and regulation of International Trade Law in Australia and internationally.
learning_outcomes: Comprehend and appreciate the law and regulatory processes applicable to international trade; particularly the relevance to sales contract law, international arbitration and international finance.
Recognise legal problems associated with international trade; use legal reasoning in the analysis of such problems; and apply legal principles to solve such problems.
Appreciate the business and social contexts in which international trade operates and is regulated.
Identify and appreciate aspects of international trade law and commerce that give rise to business, ethical and legal issues.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Semester

title: Jessup International Law Moot
syllabus_overview: Offered in conjunction with student participation in Jessup International Law Moot Competition. Students represent the Law School in this prestigious competition which involves both oral advocacy and preparation of written submissions. Students wishing to enrol in this course should first make an application to the coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Formulate and present coherent and correct legal arguments suitable for a mooting or similar environment.
Present oral presentations of legal arguments coherently and persuasively in a mooting or similar context.
Draft, explain and defend extensive written memorials in support of arguments advanced through oral advocacy.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705 + permission from Head of School

title: Comparative Law
syllabus_overview: Comparative law as an object of enquiry. Concept of legal systems and major legal systems. Construction of the civil law tradition and substantive areas of enquiry.

title: Legal History
syllabus_overview: This course is a comparative investigation into the history of the law of obligations in Australia and England. This course seeks to develop studentsÂ¿ awareness of the historical underpinnings of the modern law of obligations.

title: Advanced Crime and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course involves an advanced examination of criminal law and procedure, as well as several interrelated facets of criminology. It goes beyond the compulsory criminal law component of the LLB and places a greater focus on the causes of crime, the responses of criminal justice agencies, and justifications and critiques of criminalisation. It also introduces students to more complex aspects of substantive criminal law, including transnational crime and corporate liability. This course seeks to develop students' critical reasoning skills by encouraging them to reflect on the broader role of criminal law in society, its proper limits, and its practical operation.
learning_outcomes: Show an advanced understanding of criminal law and procedure and relevant institutional frameworks.
Identify and understand contemporary issues related to crime and criminal law, including through the lens of criminology.
Critically analyse the role of criminal law in 21st century Australian society.
Apply critical reasoning to published information and opinion.
Effectively communicate your knowledge of crime and criminal law, and related social and political issues, both in writing and verbally in ways appropriate to professional and/or academic audiences.
Locate, assess and utilise relevant information.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Clinical Legal Education
syllabus_overview: This clinical legal education course provides students with the opportunity to engage in supervised legal practice. A range of clinics will be available each semester.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply knowledge of relevant areas of law within a social justice and human rights oriented legal practice.
Research, analyse and communicate legal issues in appropriate professional formats, including written advice, letters, legal forms, and other documents.

Practise ethically and professionally within a community legal setting, including by managing records consistently with organisational practices and responding sensitively to clients’ individual circumstances.
Reflect critically on the practice of law, including the lawyer’s role in responding to clients with complex needs, and in practising in a trauma informed, client-centred, and culturally safe manner.
In client-facing clinics, interview clients, take instructions and communicate legal information and advice effectively, including in-person and by telephone.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705 and permission from Head of School

assessment_tasks.task_name: Record of student engagement: clinical days, induction and debrief sessions Hurdle In-person

workload_hours: Placement 36 Hours/ Semester

title: Law Journals
syllabus_overview: Editing of law journals, research and writing of case notes, reviews and essays for a journal and preparation of the journal for publication.
learning_outcomes: Manage the process of publishing an issue of a scholarly academic journal under the peer review process in academic publishing; edit academic articles, reviews and notes; and manage the practical aspects of timely, effective publication of the journal.
Recognise and reflect upon, and respond to, ethical issues that arise in the process of editing an academic journal including conflicts of interest and intellectual property issues.
Learn and work with autonomy, accountability and professionalism.
Reflect on and assess work of others, and make use of feedback as appropriate, to support personal and professional development.
Collaborate effectively with the Editor in Chief and the other members of the student editorial committee to manage the process of publishing the AILJ.
Communicate in ways that are effective, appropriate and persuasive with submitting authors, reviewers, the Editor in Chief and other members of the student editorial committee.
Undertake, use and synthesise international legal research.
Analyse and discuss the broad contours of international legal research relevant to the journal.

Perceive the diversity of what is generally classified as international legal research, including its underlying philosophies and approaches; and identify where your own personal legal views and approaches are placed relative to the relevant body of research; and express an informed and well-reasoned personal legal perspective or position relative to a discrete area of international legal research published in the journal.
Identify trends in international legal research, including what factors may influence those trends.
Write in a style suitable for a university international law journal publication.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Book review or Case note Online

title: Research Project A
syllabus_overview: This course provides an opportunity for students to pursue in some depth an area of special interest under the supervision of a member of the Law School academic staff. Further guidelines are available from the Law School.
learning_outcomes: Formulate a significant and novel research question in or across the fields of doctrinal law, legal theory or socio-legal studies.
Design a research project to investigate that question using appropriate approaches to legal research and methodologies.
Utilise legal writing techniques that are appropriate to different academic aims and audiences.
Manage research projects to produce quality work within time-constraints.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705 + permission from Head of School
workload_hours: Supervision

title: Islamic Law
syllabus_overview: An introduction to the history and scope of Islamic law and the legal system including an examination of comparative issues relating to Islamic and western secular legal and constitutional thought. Topics include: pre-Islamic background; features of the Islamic legal system; sources, the theoretical and practical application of Islamic law; comparative issues and Islamic criminal law and procedure.
workload_hours: Lecture 1 Hour/ Week Seminar 2 Hours/ Week

title: Copyright Law
syllabus_overview: Copyright law stands at the vanguard of the law's interaction with technology. It touches computer science, art, architecture, music, fashion, social media, broadcast media, movies and more. This course provides an in-depth examination of copyright law from its foundations and justifications through to its practical application in novel circumstances. It will develop students' knowledge of the nature and scope of copyright in Australia and will compare Australian law with that of other jurisdictions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the principles of copyright law.
Analyse and interpret the relevant statutory provisions relating to the subject matter of the course.
Identify and apply relevant legal principles to various situations.
Demonstrate skills in legal research, and written and oral communication skills, appropriate to the subject matter of the course.
Critically evaluate the implications and effectiveness of the principles of copyright law.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Presentation, Written Outline and Reflection Online

workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Immigration and Refugee Law
syllabus_overview: Immigration and Refugee Law examines the legal and regulatory framework under which persons are permitted to migrate to Australia. It examines the various migration programs (Family, Skilled, Refugee) as well as the ability of the courts to review migration decisions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a thorough understanding of Australian immigration law and international refugee law.
Demonstrate a comprehensive knowledge of the sources of migration law, including relevant legislation, case law, government sources, and scholarly writing.
Understand relevant government policies in this field and in related areas.
Understand and appreciate the situation, needs, and rights of asylum seekers, refugees, and permanent and temporary migrants.
Discuss topical socio-legal issues, about immigration and refugee law/policy in an open and respectful forum.
Identify and structure relevant socio-legal issues and present them logically.
Independently research, identify, and locate relevant information and scholarly literature of the highest quality.
Present and communicate research outcomes to an audience and (where appropriate) develop informed, coherent strategies for law reform and policy change in this field of study.
Develop alternative strategies and recommendations for law reform and policy change.
Communicate clearly and efficiently in a written paper.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705

End of semester examination Identity Verified In-person

title: Patent and Trademark Law
syllabus_overview: The course will examine patent and trademark law, which are of increasing importance to knowledge-based industries. It will consider registration criteria, protection of unregistered interests and associated legal concepts.

title: Law Moot A
syllabus_overview: This course involves mooting on a topical legal issue or field of law. Only students who have been selected through a competitive application process will be able to enrol. Course credit may be available for participation in the following competitions: Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) Moot Competition Deakin International Commercial Arbitration Moot The Hon Michael Kirby Contract Law Moot The University of Queensland Unjust Enrichment Moot UNSW Private Law Moot Sir Harry Gibbs Constitutional Law Moot Competition Willem C Vis International Arbitration Moot International Maritime Law Arbitration Moot Moot competitions vary from year to year. Please refer to the Law School's mooting webpage for information on available competitions, and the application process/timelines.
learning_outcomes: Undertake legal research and formulate legal arguments suitable for a mooting or similar environment.
Present oral arguments coherently and persuasively in a mooting or similar context.
Draft extensive written memorials in support of arguments to be advanced through oral advocacy.
Work productively with peers in accordance with legal professional norms.

Oral advocacy during practice moot (Presentation Recorded) In-person

title: Alternative Dispute Resolution
syllabus_overview: An introduction to the theories and principles of Alternate Dispute Resolution (ADR) as applied within the context of Australian legal disputes. The course provides an overview of the most well-used ADR practices including a detailed exploration of the mediation and arbitration processes most likely to be encountered in practice. Students will leave the course with a working knowledge of ADR theory and principles as well as an understanding of the importance of dispute resolution strategies in modern legal practice.
learning_outcomes: Understand and critically discuss alternate dispute resolution in an legal Australian context, and in particular how ADR fits into modern legal practice and the provision of 'justice' in contemporary society.

Be familiar with the range of dispute resolution mechanisms available as alternatives to judicial proceedings, with particular emphasis on negotiation, mediation and arbitration, and the factors governing party choice of these processes.

Demonstrate practical understanding of the steps involved in ADR processes, and have experienced the processes involved in legally assisted negotiation and mediation through practical exercises during class.
Understand the place of ADR processes within court systems, and how they interact with judicial determination.
Understand, appreciate, and be able to analyse critically legislative and other frameworks for ADR.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Workshop 30 Hours/ Semester 5 days intensive workshop

title: Law Moot B
syllabus_overview: This course involves mooting on a topical legal issue or field of law. Only students who have been selected through a competitive application process will be able to enrol. Course credit may be available for participation in the following competitions: Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) Moot Competition Deakin International Commercial Arbitration Moot The Hon Michael Kirby Contract Law Moot The University of Queensland Unjust Enrichment Moot UNSW Private Law Moot Sir Harry Gibbs Constitutional Law Moot Competition Willem C Vis International Arbitration Moot International Maritime Law Arbitration Moot Moot competitions vary from year to year. Please refer to the Law School's mooting webpage for information on available competitions, and the application process/timelines.
learning_outcomes: Undertake legal research and formulate legal arguments suitable for a mooting or similar environment.
Present oral arguments coherently and persuasively in a mooting or similar context.
Draft extensive written memorials in support of arguments to be advanced through oral advocacy.
Work productively with peers in accordance with legal professional norms.

Oral advocacy during practice moot (Presentation Recorded) In-person

title: Law of Evidence
syllabus_overview: This course is a critical examination of the law and practice relating to evidence in civil & criminal proceedings in Queensland and under the uniform legislation operating in some other parts of Australia. The course seeks to develop students' knowledge of evidence law and the ability to understand how it operates in practice. Students seeking admission to the legal profession must complete this course or its equivalent.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 10 Hours/ Semester

title: Civil Procedure
syllabus_overview: An analysis of the common law system of adversarial adjudication, including State and Federal civil court jurisdiction, costs of litigation, service of process, the role of the court in managing civil litigation, defining the questions for trial, obtaining evidence, pre-trial disclosure, disposition without trial, settling litigation, judgment and enforcing judgment, and appeals.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: The Legal Profession
syllabus_overview: An introduction to philosophies of applied ethics and to the idea of professionalism, including the structure and regulation of the legal profession, admission and discipline, and professional duties to the law, the courts, other practitioners and the client.
workload_hours: Lecture 2 Hours/ Week Tutorial 1 Hour/ Week

title: Research Project B
syllabus_overview: This course provides an opportunity for students to pursue in some depth an area of special interest under the supervision of a member of the Law School academic staff. Further guidelines are available from the Law School.

title: Special Topic B
syllabus_overview: This course will involve the study of a topical legal issue or field of law. Topics will vary from year to year. Refer to the Law School website for the current topic.
learning_outcomes: Understand the key ideas and insights of leading conceptions of justice.
Understand how theories of law and justice inform and are engaged by legal doctrine.
Think critically about how the study and practice of law implicate justice/injustice.
Demonstrate legal writing, research, and communication skills appropriate to professional and/or academic audiences.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Tort Claims Against Government - Private Remedies for Public Wrongs
syllabus_overview: Provides an in-depth study of the ways in which tort law ensures accountability and compensates for injury caused by the wrongful use of state powers. Covers state immunity, misfeasance in public office, false imprisonment, and public body negligence in key areas of social regulation and welfare provision such as policing, public health and safety, immigration detention and the protection of the mentally ill.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate detailed knowledge of the principles governing the tortious liability of public authorities for malicious prosecution, misfeasance in public office, false imprisonment and negligence (with a particular focus on the negligence liability of the police, child-protection agencies, prison and health authorities and local councils).
Demonstrate advanced problem-solving skills within the field.
Demonstrate advanced, independent research-skills within the field, including the ability to locate and reference materials beyond those provided, through use of libraries and on-line databases.
Demonstrate ability to communicate ideas and research findings effectively in writing and to observe disciplinary citation practices.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: Seminar 3 Hours/ Week

title: Personal and Corporate Insolvency
syllabus_overview: A study of the law of insolvency as applied to individuals & corporate bodies. The course will explore the rationale for, & core principles of, insolvency, the law regarding the identification of the assets of the insolvent, the avoidance of pre-insolvency transactions & the order of distribution and winding up. The course will also explore alternatives to insolvency.
learning_outcomes: Understand and apply the competing theoretical frameworks relating to the nature and purpose of personal and corporate insolvency law.
Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental principles of personal and corporate insolvency law in Australia and the policy reasons for the existence of those principles.
Critically analyse the efficacy and utility of the principles of personal and corporate insolvency law in Australia.
Apply the principles of personal and corporate insolvency law in Australia to a variety of different factual problem based circumstances.
prerequisites: All Level 1 and 2 LAWS courses + LAWS3700 + LAWS3705
workload_hours: 5 day seminar

title: Special Topic C
syllabus_overview: This course will involve the study of a topical legal issue or field of law. Topics will vary from year to year. Refer to the Law School website for the current topic.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate strong proficiency in the editing, proofreading and formatting-for-publication of academic articles.
Apply the Australian Guide to Legal Citation (AGLC) accurately and consistently, in line with the Journal’s internal policies and style guides.

Explain the different legal approaches that underpin legal protections of individual privacy.

title: Law of Political Institutions
syllabus_overview: This course is an intermediate level elective on the structure and rationale of parliamentary democracy and elections. It offers a detailed examination of the regulation of political participants, finances and electoral processes. The course will be taught in a theoretical and contextual manner, with particular attention to values such as political equality and competitiveness. It seeks to develop an understanding of the pivotal but under-appreciated role of legal norms in shaping representative democracy.
learning_outcomes: Explain, and research more deeply, the important features of the regulation of parliament, elections and political activity.
Structure and argue essay, seminar discussion and exam problems, applying both practical and theoretical considerations relevant to the course.
Understand the role that law and institutions play in regulating representative democracy.
Integrate the institutions and rules studied into their political and normative contexts: those contexts are important to an understanding of - and potential reform in - this field.
